Chapter 10: The Lingering Shadow—Segregation’s Legacy Today.
Even though it’s been decades since the most obvious forms of housing discrimination were banned, their effects haven’t just disappeared. You can still sense those old boundaries—they might not be drawn on maps the same way, but they haven’t vanished. Instead, they’ve found new shapes in our neighborhoods and daily routines.
Picture this: a teenager today, walking the same blocks their grandparents once did. They notice the contrasts from one neighborhood to the next—how some schools have brand-new facilities, while others struggle to keep the lights on. Some parks feel welcoming and safe, while others are neglected. Maybe the nearest grocery store is just down the street… or maybe it’s miles away. That teenager might not know the full history, but they definitely feel its impact every day.
The gap in wealth between Black and white families? It’s still there. That’s not just a number—it reflects who was able to buy homes, build equity, and pass down resources, and who was systematically shut out. Schools in areas that were once redlined continue to face underfunding, while those in more affluent neighborhoods thrive. And it goes beyond just money—health, job prospects, even how long people live, are all shaped by the places they call home.
Sure, some cities are stepping up. They’re investing in affordable housing, tweaking zoning rules, or creating programs to help more families buy homes. But this is slow, tough work—and those old patterns don’t break easily. The legacy of segregation isn’t just tucked away in history books; it’s still woven into our everyday lives.
Most of us don’t realize just how much the past is shaping our present. We notice the differences, but not the decisions that carved them out. That lingering shadow of segregation? It’s a reminder that the work of creating a fairer society is still unfolding—and that each of us has a part to play in moving it forward.
